title: Zelda: Ocarina of Time’s Coolest Dungeon Hides a Secret Tribute to a Beloved Classic
author: @hellojenglen
content:
Follow

Link copied to clipboard

Published Nov 9, 2026, 4:05 PM EST

The world is hard on ambitious girls

Sign in to your Polygon.com account

Nintendo's highly anticipated remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is finally here, and millions of players are reliving their childhood adventures or experiencing Link's journey for the very first time. Though the Nintendo 64 game has received a dramatic visual glow-up for the Switch 2, the remake meticulously preserves the spirit of the original — including an extended reference to a classic American novel that even Ocarina diehards may have missed the first time around.

[Ed. note: Mid-game spoilers ahead for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. If you haven't retrieved the Master Sword yet, turn back now!]

After Link collects the three Spiritual Stones and returns to Hyrule Castle Town to claim the Master Sword, we move forward seven years in time. Link is now an adult, and in order to thwart Ganon's terrifying reign, he must awaken six sages throughout Hyrule by visiting their temples and claiming their power for his own. The first of these is located just outside Link's hometown of Kokiri Village, land of the fairy folk. Though most of his youthful pals don't recognize the grown-up Link, they urge him to investigate the Forest Temple and rescue their dear friend Saria.

When Link ventures into the Forest Temple, he discovers something altogether unexpected: an eerie, luxurious old mansion inhabited by ghosts. As he enters a central room flanked by colorful torches, four ghostly Poes appear to snatch away the flames. Venturing deeper into the mansion, Link discovers that these ghoulish gals are actually four sisters: Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy.

Sound familiar? Those are the same names (and the same birth order) as the March sisters in Louisa May Alcott's novel Little Women. It's a timeless coming-of-age story about four sisters who have very different goals and ambitions in life, one that's been adapted countless times for stage and screen. The most recent adaptation is the 2019 film by Barbie and The Magician's Nephew director Greta Gerwig, which stars Saoirse Ronan, Florence Pugh, and Timothée Chalamet.

While you might be inclined to think this is some newfangled meddling with the localization, these were also the Poe Sisters' names in the Nintendo 64 original. (There's one exception: the second sister, Jo, was called "Joelle" in the 1998 game.) Naturally, there are plenty of "well actually" guys pointing this out in the comments of social media posts. But it's still a fun little Easter egg for players discovering it for the first time, whether or not they've played Ocarina of Time before.

If you're like me and have never played Ocarina of Time until now, be sure to check out Polygon's extensive guides and walkthroughs for the remake. Like this hidden node, there are plenty of puzzle solutions, hidden items, and valuable power-ups you can easily miss on your first playthrough.

title: Apple’s $50 Intelligence Usage Packs extend access to some AI features
author: Andrew Liszewski
content:
Andrew Liszewski

is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

After publishing a support article in early September outlining usage limits for some Apple Intelligence features, the company has updated Logic Pro with an option to “Buy More Usage” for a one-time purchase price of $49.99, as spotted by 9to5Mac. It has a built-in AI assistant to do things like “start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project.”

These Intelligence Usage Packs, as Apple calls them, will allow users to continue accessing certain Apple Intelligence features that have usage limits because they rely on cloud-based AI models from OpenAI or Google Gemini. The Usage Packs can only be used by the Apple Account that purchased them (Family Sharing isn’t supported) and, as Apple explains on its website, any unused additional usage will roll over from month to month, but will expire 12 months after it was purchased.

For Logic Pro, Apple says the usage limit is “impacted by the complexity of conversations you have with the assistant.” Users finding themselves running out of access can find the option to buy an Intelligence Usage Pack in the Intelligence Features > Show Usage section of the app’s main menu. Currently, only Logic Pro has the option to buy more usage, but it’s expected to be added to other Apple Creator Studio apps this month, including Pixelmator Pro, Final Cut Pro, Motion, plus Pages, Keynote, and Numbers that are getting access to Apple’s AI chatbot.

title: Why Are We So Good at Feeling Bad?
author: @NewYorker
content:
A behavioral economist sets out to explain why we’re so prone to overreacting and spiralling.

November 9, 2026

“At the heart of so many of our miseries,” George Loewenstein says, “is not the fact that we feel bad, but the belief that we should feel otherwise.” Our brains fight with themselves.Illustration by Tim Enthoven

Charles Darwin was not a well man. As a youth, he suffered from scarlet fever and eczema. He couldn’t stand the sight of blood at medical school, and his five-year voyage on the Beagle brought seasickness, headaches, and infections. After returning to England, in 1836, he developed severe anxiety and gastrointestinal issues, including bouts of vomiting and flatulence. He also suffered from insomnia, fatigue, and depression.

In 1849, ten years before he published “On the Origin of Species,” he wrote to a friend of “dreadful vomiting every week” and reported, “I was not able to do anything one day out of three.” He thought that he was “rapidly going the way of all flesh.” In fact, he lived another thirty-three years, though the ailments never left him. Giving a scientific paper, or even attending a party, could overwhelm him. By then, he had moved to a village in Kent, rarely venturing out without his wife, Emma.

From 1849 to 1855, Darwin kept a “diary of health,” recording his conditions as “goodish,” “poorish,” and “very bad fl[atulence] with fright.” He consulted some twenty doctors and tried Victorian cures, including hydrotherapy, which offered some relief, and galvanism. Diagnoses included nervous dyspepsia, water brash (acid reflux), and “suppressed gout” (whatever that is).

What was the problem? Retrospective diagnoses range from Chagas’ disease, a parasitic illness he might have contracted in South America, to lactose intolerance. He may have suffered from some combination of diseases and allergies, and possibly Crohn’s. But some symptoms suggest a psychological condition. Agoraphobia with panic disorder is a plausible diagnosis.

Whatever the cause or causes, Darwin must, at some point, have asked himself, I got naturally selected for this? Of course, not every affliction has an evolutionary purpose. People get sick. But our extraordinary susceptibility to misery does raise a question about what kind of creatures natural selection has made us. We get depressed when we win the lottery; we lie awake worrying about whether the car needs new tires; we feel jealous when our girlfriend talks too long with the barista.

Anxiety might have adaptive utility when we are in danger of being eaten by a sabre-toothed tiger. But there are not a lot of sabre-toothed tigers around anymore, and we still get anxious, frequently for no very good reason. We don’t just react emotionally to things. We overreact. Why have genes for emotional overreaction, rather than genes for being cool, calm, and collected, been passed along? Wouldn’t we be reproductively fitter if we weren’t unhappy so much of the time?

These are questions George Loewenstein tries to answer in “The Opposite of Happiness: How Bad Feelings Make and Break Us” (Harper). Loewenstein, who teaches at Carnegie Mellon, is a leader in the field of behavioral economics. Neoclassical economics relied on the fiction of the rational actor, someone who makes decisions by way of a judicious calculation of self-interest. Behavioral economics, by contrast, emphasizes the nonrational factors in economic decision-making. Whatever human beings are rational about, it’s not money. We overspend it; we under-save it; we buy stuff on impulse. We generally don’t do the math. Why it took so long for this to dawn on economists is mystifying. Didn’t those people ever read a novel? Virtually every famous nineteenth-century novel is about people behaving badly around money.

Still, figuring out why we act foolishly when we could, or should, or want to act otherwise is a worthy academic pursuit. Among Loewenstein’s contributions is the identification of what he calls “empathy gaps,” our inability to imagine how we would feel or behave in an emotional state different from the one we’re in. When we’re pain-free, we can’t really remember what pain feels like. When we’re angry, we can’t imagine being calm. Emotions, Loewenstein argues, can reprogram our whole psyche. He gives a personal example: learning that it is better to wait a day before responding to an annoying e-mail.

Didn’t we know this already, though? Adam Smith made similar observations in “The Theory of Moral Sentiments” (1759). And some of Loewenstein’s work does seem to amount to a confirmation of common sense. One of his experiments, for instance, measured the effect of sexual arousal on judgment and decision-making in male students. Guess what? A sexually aroused young man reported a greater willingness to engage in morally questionable behavior to obtain sexual gratification.

Explaining how feelings affect our judgment is one thing. Why so many emotions make us unhappy is another. That’s the larger question Loewenstein takes up. His thesis is that these emotions “were built to keep us alive and reproducing, not to keep us happy.”

Loewenstein is hardly alone in proposing evolutionary explanations for misery. Randolph M. Nesse, a psychiatrist, made a similar case in “Good Reasons for Bad Feelings: Insights from the Frontier of Evolutionary Psychiatry” (2019), a work Loewenstein discusses. Such arguments recall the “selfish gene” model. Evolution is not about the reproduction of persons, is the idea. It’s about the reproduction of genes. And, from a gene’s point of view, the body is just a disposable gene container. It can fret about the tires, climb the Matterhorn, write “On the Origin of Species”—whatever, as long as the genes keep getting passed along. Darwin may have been wretched much of the time, but he had ten children. He checked the evolutionary box. Was he also farting and throwing up a lot? Sure. His genes didn’t care.

But Loewenstein thinks that negative emotions aren’t simply a design flaw or a regrettable by-product of natural selection. On the contrary, he thinks that we have good evolutionary reasons for being able to feel bad. Our ancestors would have been less “fit” to pass their genes along if they hadn’t been equipped with negative emotions. Fear could save us from predators; guilt could help us maintain the social bonds on which survival depended.

Knowing this, Loewenstein warns, won’t make us feel any less unhappy. “I offer in these pages no tips and precious little advice,” he writes. “This is not a self-help book.” (I wonder whether his publishers tried to talk him out of that.) Loewenstein describes the book as, instead, “one scientist’s bird’s-eye view of the subject, shaped by broad reading, personal experience, and, in many cases, my own research.”

“The Opposite of Happiness” is fairly nontechnical. There is no talk of neurotransmitters, and Loewenstein, who has himself conducted brain-imaging research, thinks that the interpretation of functional-MRI scans is often “not much more reliable than reading tea leaves.” The book is also quite personal, although selectively so. Loewenstein lets us know, for example, that he suffers from paruresis (shy-bladder syndrome) but neglects to mention that he is a great-grandson of Sigmund Freud, whose theories of unconscious drives bear some family resemblance to Loewenstein’s account of our emotional programming.

The problem with a lot of evolutionary psychology is that its explanations are hard to verify. It undertakes to explain an observable fact (we fret about bald tires) with an unobservable one (cavemen worried that a mastodon might trample them). Loewenstein is alert to the danger of producing “just-so” stories, accounts of human attributes based on unconfirmable hunches about what life was like in the Paleolithic era. But they’re hard to avoid.

Even if we accept these evolutionary explanations, they leave a further puzzle. Why do negative emotions so often persist long after they’ve served their purpose? Like the earworms of cheesy pop songs, they can get stuck in our heads. Our brains continue pumping them out even when the occasions for them have passed.

We also have the unfortunate ability to reëxperience some negative feelings just by remembering the occasions for them. We may find it hard to recall what physical pain felt like once it has stopped, but, when we remember something shameful we did, we can feel the shame all over again. Most of us could use an empathy gap there.

“At the heart of so many of our miseries,” Loewenstein says, “is not the fact that we feel bad, but the belief that we should feel otherwise.” Our brains fight with themselves. We feel ashamed of our shame, angry about our anger. The wish to escape an unpleasant emotion becomes another source of misery. Who’s running the show in there?

Not “us.” We may resolve, after firing off an intemperate e-mail, to respond more calmly the next time. But, when the next provocation arrives, our anger can make the resolution seem lame. As Loewenstein explains, we are adept at psychological self-sabotage. Sometimes our very efforts to gain control make things worse, as when athletes concentrate too intently on not trying so hard.

In the second half of “The Opposite of Happiness,” Loewenstein lets unhappiness sufferers speak for themselves. He has gathered their stories through what he calls the Misery Survey, in which more than five hundred respondents were asked about their experiences of negative emotions. Each was assigned an emotion at random and asked whether it had caused them misery. If it had, they were invited to describe the experience; if not, they were assigned another emotion. The stories make for fun reading (more or less), not so much because they hold surprises but because we recognize ourselves in so many of them. Misery, it turns out, loves company.

Loewenstein devotes a chapter to each of twelve varieties of misery. It’s a bit like Dante’s Inferno if Dante had modelled his work on the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders rather than the “Summa Theologiae” of Thomas Aquinas. The first two circles in Loewenstein’s hell are Impatience and Boredom, followed by Anger, Envy, Jealousy, Rejection, Guilt, Shame, Anxiety, Regret, Loneliness, and, in the last circle, Depression, which he deems “a fitting finale to this Hieronymus Bosch underworld of psychic torments—not just because it is so supremely awful, but because nearly all the other miseries, when they persist and accumulate, can give rise to it.” (Hate, a resurgent political emotion across much of the planet, did not make the list. Neither did grief.)

Loewenstein suspects that depression, unlike some other negative emotions, has no adaptive function of its own. It arises, he thinks, as a by-product of other psychological systems in distress. That’s close to what Peter D. Kramer concluded in his 2005 book, “Against Depression,” where he defines depression as “a disease in which a host of injuries combine to cause a common downstream process that becomes self-sustaining.” It is hard to see how suicidality conduces to reproductive success. And depression can create what Loewenstein terms “the ultimate empathy gap”: people in its grip find it almost impossible to imagine what life without it would feel like.

At the other end of his inferno is boredom. We might not think of boredom as an emotion. It seems more like the absence of emotion. But, in a study tracking the daily feelings of some four thousand adults, Loewenstein and his colleagues found that boredom frequently accompanied strong negative feelings, including anger and anxiety. “We found that boredom was 4.2 times more likely to occur in the presence of another negative emotion than a positive one,” he says.

Two places where people commonly report being bored are doctors’ waiting rooms and airport terminals. We sit there fiddling with our smartphones, and with nothing else to do, running scary or angry scenarios through our heads—the medical news will not be good, the flight will be cancelled, they will close the gate while I’m in line at Starbucks—and composing powerfully cogent letters to the airline about the incompetence of the gate crew. We get mad when we are forced to wait for something for which there are no substitutes, and then we complain that we’re bored. (In a section titled “Why Are Dreams So Boring?,” Loewenstein says that one of the most “excruciatingly boring” things we can do is listen to someone describe a dream they had. This reads like a barely veiled put-down of his famous forebear.)

But how did we acquire the capacity for boredom? There don’t seem to have been airports or doctors’ offices back in Paleolithic times, when men just hunted and gathered (and, we hope, partied). Loewenstein suggests that the ability to become bored developed as a way of budgeting attention. “If early humans didn’t feel the urge to redirect their attention when staring at the same patch of woods,” he says, “they might have missed important opportunities—a rustle in the bush that signaled prey, or an approaching threat. Our ancestors who were better at reallocating attention had an adaptive advantage: they probably avoided more predators, found more food, and pursued more socially or intellectually engaging activities.” This might be a little just-so-y. It’s hard to see how the humans or proto-humans who never got bored were the ones who got selected out. Maybe sabre-toothed tigers ate them all.

Other evolutionary explanations seem more persuasive. Loewenstein agrees with many people who have written about negative emotions that feelings like shame and guilt perform a regulatory social function. They help enforce the norms of the group. Shame, in particular, encourages submission rather than confrontation, a response “designed to protect us from one of the greatest threats to our survival—being cast out.”

Explaining why negative emotions might have evolved, though, still leaves that problem of why they can become so consuming, so hard to toggle off. Why do we spiral? Is it because we inherited emotions like anxiety which evolved in response to genuine threats to survival and can now be triggered by the prospect of missing the bus? Or were our emotions always liable to become excessive? Did our Stone Age ancestors lie awake wondering whether they had remembered to put out the fire pit?

Loewenstein thinks that it’s at least partly the latter. Our emotional system, he says, “is prone, almost by design, to malfunction.” To protect us against threats, it has to be highly sensitive, prone to false alarms rather than risk missing a real danger. But this sensitivity also makes the system unstable. He believes our psyches are poised on a “razor’s edge” between negative feedback, which allows an emotion to subside when the threat has passed, and positive feedback, in which an emotion amplifies itself. Anxiety, for example, makes us more alert to threats, which can make us perceive more threats, which heightens our anxiety. It’s like driving on an icy road: the harder we brake, the more we lose control of the car.

Of course, an emotion that makes us miserable is not necessarily an irrational response to our circumstances. One question we can ask about psychological diagnoses is whether some states we classify as symptoms of mental disorders are responses to a world that’s genuinely frightening or depressing. What if life really is meaningless? What if other people really are out to get us? What if the barista really is hitting on our girlfriend? Then feelings like sadness, anger, and jealousy might be perfectly understandable, and the emotions that need to be explained are optimism, tolerance, and a sense of humor. Maybe it’s the optimists who are the crazy ones.

In the list of books that helped replace a theological understanding of the universe with a secular one, “On the Origin of Species” is near the top. One theory about Darwin’s poor health, in fact, was that he was horrified by the implications of his own discoveries—that our species was not a special creation and that no providence dictated its characteristics. Natural selection is a blind process. There is no being out there or up there that oversees its course.

Still, there is a way in which evolutionary psychology belongs to a religious tradition, the tradition of theodicy. This was the effort of theologians to explain why, given an omnipotent and beneficent God, there is evil in the world. Transposed to a Darwinian world view, this becomes the question: If natural selection has equipped us to survive and reproduce, why has it burdened us with so much misery? There is a temptation to assume that every form of suffering must have served some evolutionary purpose, just as God must have had a reason for earthquakes in Lisbon. The problem of why bad things happen kept intellectuals busy for centuries. The problem of unhappiness promises to do the same. It may be that both depend on a shared illusion: that it all makes sense. ♦

title: Breaking the Decade-Long Trump Fever
author: @NewYorker
content:
Two generations ago, in the fall of 1974, President Gerald Ford and the Republican Party approached the midterm elections with considerable dread. That August, Richard Nixon had learned that he could no longer outrun his crimes in the White House. One tape recording in particular, the so-called smoking gun, proved that he had conspired with his aide H. R. Haldeman to obstruct the investigation into the Watergate break-in. The Republican elders Barry Goldwater, John Rhodes, and Hugh Scott told Nixon that impeachment in the House of Representatives was now certain, and conviction in the Senate likely. Nixon resigned, handing over his office to Vice-President Ford. A month later, Ford issued Proclamation 4311, pardoning Nixon for any crimes that he might have committed as President. Watergate, Ford said, had been “an American tragedy, in which we all have played a part. It could go on and on and on, or someone must write the end to it. I have concluded that only I can do that, and if I can, I must.”

Until then, despite a dreadful economy, Ford had enjoyed approval ratings as high as seventy per cent. But the Nixon pardon was political poison, for both Ford and the G.O.P. His popularity plummeted by more than twenty points. And, in the midterms, the Democrats gained forty-nine seats in the House and four seats in the Senate. The incoming class of rookie Democrats—among them Gary Hart, Paul Tsongas, John Glenn, and Patrick Leahy—became known as the “Watergate babies.”

This week, some commentators, having exhausted the usual marine metaphors for midterm blowouts (a “blue wave” quickly became a “blue tsunami”), scurried to find historical points of comparison for the astonishing nationwide triumph of the Democratic Party. More than a few settled on the post-pardon midterms of 1974.

In sheer magnitude, this week’s Democratic victory—a sweeping repudiation, above all, of Donald Trump and the low, dishonest decade he has defined—makes the post-Watergate humbling seem modest. Both houses of Congress flipped, giving Democrats a substantial majority in each. The new Senate Majority Leader needn’t worry if, say, John Fetterman strolls across party lines. Nine of the ten most populous states will have Democratic governors. For those already anticipating the Presidential race in 2028, it’s significant that all the traditional battleground states (which Trump won just two years ago) have elected Democratic governors. The Party scored in unlikely places, particularly in the Midwest and the South. Texas, the second most populous state in the Union and reliably red for a generation, will have a Democratic senator (James Talarico), governor (Gina Hinojosa), and state House. Kansas—seriously, Kansas—elected a Democrat to the Senate for the first time in ninety-four years. Democrats also chalked up amazing wins in both Carolinas. The geographic shift was as pronounced as the demographic one. After moving toward Trump in 2024, many Latinos swung Democratic; so did many young white men. (Thanks for rethinking things, Joe Rogan!) And Black voters came out for Democratic candidates in huge numbers.

The diversity of “firsts” was heartening. The first Muslim in the Senate: Abdul El-Sayed, of Michigan. The first Black female governor: Keisha Lance Bottoms, in Georgia. The first Latino governors to be elected in Texas (Hinojosa) and California (Xavier Becerra). New Mexico will have the first female Native American governor (Deb Haaland), and Minnesota will send the first Native American woman ever to the Senate (Peggy Flanagan). Even the near-misses were stunners. In ruby-red Florida, a Black democratic socialist named Angie Nixon almost became a senator. (And maybe she would have won had she gotten more funding, or had she been three jots less far to the left—hard to know.) This all happened after years in which the President and the Vice-President have deployed racist epithets, jokes, and myths. (“In Springfield, they’re eating the dogs! . . . They’re eating the cats!”) Laura Loomer, a court bigot for the Administration, made the Trumpian ideology clear when she wrote on X, “America was always intended to be a majority White country. Not a cesspool for third world minorities. America was founded as a Christian country. Not a Muslim country.” The midterms dealt that foul idea its greatest blow since Barack Obama’s ascent to the Presidency, in 2008.

The scale of the victory left no room for Trump to contrive a conspiracy theory and challenge the outcome. On Election Night, he was, by his perverse standards, gracious. He blamed Fox News for the Republican losses, “by constantly and consistently putting on the Dumocrat opposition.” Separately, he claimed, “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” #Classic.

The results were driven by the most urgent economic concerns of the voters: the spike in fuel prices, which followed the misbegotten tariffs and the war in Iran; the high cost of groceries, housing, and health care; and, for some, anxiety about data centers, artificial intelligence, and what all this portends for employment. But what is so striking about Trump’s second term is that he entered office intent, it now seems, on flaunting his cynicism, his greed, and his scorn for the American people. It was as if he actually meant to squander his support as quickly as possible. How else to explain the heedlessness of his behavior in office? On Day One, he gave pride of place at the Inauguration to a lineup of moguls who had agreed to bow to his power and his ego. They regularly traipsed to the White House, delivering gaudy house gifts and large donations to his pet projects. They smiled weakly as they were compelled to listen to his moronic rants and admire the latest ungapatchka embellishment of the gilded Oval Office. They spent tens of millions of dollars on his wife’s documentary about how taxing it is to endure the attentions of the help and how lonely it is to shuttle from one place to the next in limousines and private planes. As in any tin-pot autocracy, this was the price of doing business. Trump’s populism was always a fraud. Now he plainly didn’t care who knew. At a “jungle-themed” Halloween party at Mar-a-Lago, costumed guests enjoyed seafood delicacies and a caviar bar. There was a caged zebra. Circus performers dangled from the ceiling. “Rich people, they spend nine hours getting ready,” the President merrily remarked of his pals. He was dressed in his usual blue suit. “I had ten minutes, so I came as Donald Trump.”

Trump has shown contempt for the law, as he hollowed out the Department of Justice and ordered federal agents to menace American cities from New York to Minneapolis to Los Angeles. He has shown contempt for culture and education, as he threatened and defunded one invaluable institution after another. He has shown contempt for competence, by stocking his Administration with preposterous, often odious, fourth-raters: Pete Hegseth, Kash Patel, Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., Kristi Noem, Stephen Miller (incredibly, the new chief of staff), the Son-in-Law, the Ubiquitous One with the portable printer.

Abroad, Trump’s contempt for restraints on his power has been equally conspicuous. The United States’ closest allies found themselves coping with his arbitrary tariffs, his threats to shatter alliances, and his periodic intimations of invasion. What was the world to make of an American President who, with immense self-satisfaction, slathered praise on dictators like Vladimir Putin, Viktor Orbán, and Xi Jinping, while seeking to humiliate heroic democrats like Volodymyr Zelensky? Trump ordered his government to invade Venezuela, imprison its President, elevate a more compliant one, and start extracting that nation’s oil and gold. It was a regression to an earlier era of U.S. imperialism, when military intervention in Latin America was a standard instrument of Presidential power.

The most consequential result of the midterms has been to break the fever of Trumpism and to diminish its threat to democratic institutions, to personal and civil liberties, and to decency itself. Trump’s unique brand of lurid authoritarianism has finally lost appeal, and he has lost the plot. The election was also a vindication for those who had refused to submit. We are all too familiar by now with the many politicians, law partners, billionaires, C.E.O.s, university presidents, and others who cowered before Trump. Part of the reason we will survive the Trump era is that many more did their work honorably. Judges, civil-rights lawyers, academics, election officials, curators, artists, and countless ordinary citizens stood up. Their resistance to Trump’s bullying, corruption, and heartlessness has gained new political force.

After the midterms, the White House issued a “PSA” on social media: “Trump is still your president.” That is useful information. While he remains in office, his party is unlikely to rid itself of its cultlike obedience. J. D. Vance, his would-be successor, believes that he can win in two years simply by acknowledging the folly of going to war with Iran, while still aping the cruelty and dogma of his mentor. It is Vance’s conviction, he has said, that “Donald Trump will ultimately decide who’s going to be the Republican nominee.”

This is a moment of enormous relief and celebration. Trump can still do damage, and, in defeat, may prove even more unhinged and vengeful. But restraints in Congress and beyond are now far stronger. This aging autocrat, repudiated by an electorate he once believed to be under his spell, has been significantly weakened.

The Watergate babies arrived in Washington in 1975 resolved to transform American politics; when Jimmy Carter, a moderate Democrat, won the Presidency, their prospects seemed to brighten even more. Yet, just six years after their great electoral triumph, Ronald Reagan, a right-wing ideologue, was elected President and the Republicans captured the Senate. The reformers of 1974 found themselves defending gains they had expected to build on. They had helped change Washington, but the country was changing in ways they struggled to understand. The next Congress will succeed not through an obsession with retribution and punishment but by delivering on the myriad hopes and demands of the voters who elected its members. The Democrats of 2026 have won an extraordinary opportunity. What they make of it will determine what this election means. ♦

title: A New Species Emerges From a 9.5 Million-Year-Old Whale Carcass - Nautilus
content:
When a whale dies and sinks to the bottom of the ocean, its carcass becomes a banquet for smaller marine organisms, supplying food for decades. It’s a perfect example of the circle of life—and also a decent way to discover new species able to survive solely because of these so-called whale falls.

In fact, researchers recently found a constellation of new brittle star fossils near a whale fall that dates back some 9.5 million years.

Read more: “Are Killer Whales Also Cannibals?”

As described in a newly published study, researchers first discovered an ancient beaked whale—specifically fossils of a lower jaw and four vertebrae from the same carcass—in the Gram clay pit in southern Denmark, which was once part of the North Sea.

The whale bones were found in 2018, but it’s only just now that the brittle star species has been identified. These slender-armed, distant relatives of starfish have been around for millions of years, but this is thought to be the earliest brittle star to ever be uncovered at a whale fall feast. 

While the researchers can’t say for certain that the brittle star turned up for the whale buffet, it seems likely. Other samples collected farther from the whale remains, for instance, had none of the brittle star skeletal plates. “We considered whether currents had simply concentrated the plates around the bones, or whether local chemical conditions had helped preserve them,” study author Ben Thuy said in a statement. “However, sea-urchin fragments of comparable size and mineral composition occurred in every sample studied. This makes a preservation-only explanation less likely and supports the interpretation that the brittle stars lived on or close to the whale carcass.”

The new species has been named Ophiura huebnerjenseni, in honor of Holger Hübner and Thomas Jensen, founders of the Wacken Open Air heavy metal festival in Germany—an event notorious for its muddy conditions, not dissimilar to the mud that this new brittle star has been preserved in for millennia.

title: Traveling Route 66 in the Age of Data Centers
author: Cheri Lucas Rowlands
content:
In its heyday, Route 66 was a road of opportunities and dreams. Today, it’s a highway of ghosts, a symbol of what once was, although it still attracts visitors. For Current Affairs, Jesse Wright reflects on America’s historic highway in a time of artificial intelligence, when so much land across the country is being bought up, repurposed, and turned into data centers. Wright, who traveled the road from Chicago to Santa Monica, asks: What will these massive centers leave behind?

But what is new, perhaps, is the utter absence of even having been at all. The data centers’ legacy will be nothing. Their absence will be complete. Computer hallucinations leave no room for the dreams of humans. In 100 years, there will be nothing. Nobody will want to spend their vacation touring endless rooms full of rusty server racks.

title: A Rare Chance to See a Turner Masterpiece Up Very Close
author: @NewYorker
content:
Racking up the air miles, requiring no sleep, and still in tremendous shape, a distinguished visitor—a real piece of work—is arriving in New York and staying on Madison Avenue. Callers will be received from Saturday, November 7th, through Wednesday the 18th. High rollers are especially welcome, but anyone can come.

“Rome, from Mount Aventine” is an oil painting by Turner—or, to give him his full due, Joseph Mallord William Turner, R.A. It measures just over three feet by four; owners of a fifty-five-inch TV will have a rough idea of the size, although the colors in the Turner would make the engineers at Samsung break down and cry. Should you wish to install the work in your home, the happy news is that it needs no internet connection; the only slight drawback is that it may cost you north of sixty-seven million dollars. That is the conservative estimate placed on the painting by Sotheby’s, in whose New York branch it will temporarily hang, before going under the gavel at the company’s London auction house, on December 9th. Somebody, somewhere, is going to have a poorer but happier Christmas.

Nowadays, it is not uncommon for single paintings awaiting sale to go on tour like rock stars. “Salvator Mundi”—a portrait of Jesus, which, depending on your taste and your scholarly instinct, was wholly or partly or minimally painted by Leonardo da Vinci—travelled to Hong Kong, London, San Francisco, and Singapore before being hawked at Christie’s in New York, in 2017. It sold for more than four hundred and fifty million dollars and then went quiet; reportedly, it now resides in Saudi Arabia, although, for all we know, it could be hanging out at the Chateau Marmont and running up a bar tab for the ages. Similarly, “Rome, from Mount Aventine” has been on the road. Before New York, it was in Hong Kong; before Hong Kong, in London; and, before London, in Rome, where it was displayed in lonely splendor at the Palazzo Rondinini, between the River Tiber and the Villa Borghese gardens. The painting was, so to speak, returning to its place of birth.

The date of that birth is not easy to pin down. The first stirrings of “Rome, from Mount Aventine” can be traced to a trip that Turner made to Italy in 1828, the third of seven visits to the country. At the age of fifty-three, he arrived in Rome in October, having set off from England in August. (Imprudently, he delayed his return until January, 1829. When his stagecoach foundered in the alpine snows, Turner calmly rendered the scene in a dramatic watercolor; what was a disaster for his fellow-travellers was, for him, an aesthetic opportunity.) During his months in the city, he made several intricate sketches that would contribute to “Rome, from Mount Aventine.” By good fortune, they still exist, in the possession of London’s Tate Gallery, and can be compared with the finished painting. But how long was it in the finishing?

If you want to see a field of battle being keenly contested, try the dating of paintings by art historians. Quarrels over dates are not as lethally implacable as quarrels over attribution—who painted what?—but, then, nothing is. The fact that the wood of the frame over which “Rome, from Mount Aventine” is stretched, for instance, appears to be of Italian manufacture could mean that Turner began mapping out the work in Rome. If so, he must have had it in mind, and perhaps in hand, by the time he left the place, and then gone back to the canvas in the years to come, though the pattern of his labors is unclear. Turner was hardly alone among artists in devoting the same intensity of care to the enrichment of a painting that others give to the rearing of a child.

What we do know is that the painting was finally exhibited at the Royal Academy, in London, in 1836, and that it was bought by Hugh Munro, one of Turner’s most important patrons, who had originally commissioned it. Munro was a fascinating specimen: a wealthy Scot, though not a nobleman, he didn’t lord it over Turner so much as befriend him, despite being more than twenty years his junior, and the two of them even journeyed through France and Italy together, drawing and painting as they went, with the artist acting as his patron’s informal tutor. A shy soul, Munro had inherited his fortune via an uncle only after the untimely death of the latter’s sons. One was killed by a tiger and the other by a shark.

So, what did Munro get for his money, when he bought “Rome, from Mount Aventine”? An amalgam of the precise and the visionary, such as Turner alone could concoct. We find ourselves on the southernmost of the city’s seven hills, the Aventine, gazing at once downward, across, and afar. Immediately below us, a bald-headed friar passes; a young woman greets him on her knees, raising her hands in supplication. Miles away, in the distance, on the left, another dome—that of St. Peter’s—breaks the horizon and rhymes with the friar’s pate. In between is the slow, broad blue-violet curve of the Tiber, whose waters seem to rise like vapors and cling to the buildings on the shore: a capillary action, and an ideal match for the way in which the Roman past, refusing to evaporate, insists on climbing and sticking to the stones, and the human lives, of the present day.

The painting is commanded by an umbrella pine, which arches high into the butter-yellow heavens, on the right, leaning over the heart of the composition. Framing by tree is a well-worn trick, perfected by Claude Lorrain, whom Turner revered, and deployed by Turner long before he ever went to Rome (as in his depiction of Aeneas and the Cumaean Sibyl, from 1814-15, now housed in the Yale Center for British Art). The slanting trunk of the pine, in “Rome, from Mount Aventine,” is answered, at a near-right angle, on the left, by a not quite horizontal block of white, set back from the river. This is the Ospizio di San Michele a Ripa, in Trastevere. Approach the painting, close enough to see the scratchy hatchings with which Turner enlivens the walls and roofs of the riverside dwellings, and you will notice three tiny awnings, left open, on the Ospizio’s long façade: grace notes to interrupt any threat of monotone. Our eyes deserve to be occupied.

All this was too much for some early viewers. The painting was disdained, by a critic in Blackwood’s magazine, as “a most unpleasant mixture, wherein white gambouge and raw sienna are, with childish execution, daubed together.” Gambouge, or gamboge, is a toxic yellow-gold pigment derived from resin. In other words, the quality that now pulls us most startlingly into “Rome, from Mount Aventine”—its all-pervading luminescence—is exactly what unnerved the reviewer, who claimed that Turner “has robbed the sun of its birthright to cast shadows.” As so often, hostility is more suggestive than acclaim; despite the darkness in the southeast quarter of the painting, it is overbearingly bright, as if the Eternal City were itself a source of light. In a postscript to the controversy, the young John Ruskin was so incensed by the article in Blackwood’s that he leaped to the defense of Turner, who forwarded his broadside to Munro. It was the opening salvo in what would become Ruskin’s lifelong campaign to appraise, and to praise, Turner’s art. If you buy this painting, therefore, you are getting not just a glorious staging post in Turner’s career, plus a chapter in the long saga of Italy worship, but, also, for what it’s worth, a footnote in the history of criticism.

In mid-October, in London, I spent an hour with “Rome, from Mount Aventine.” To see it in the flesh is to realize how much blood is lost in even the most exacting of reproductions. The scumbled clouds at the top left, barely perceptible on the page of a book, could be read as more Venetian than Roman—rose-pink against blue, as in the dawn sky of a Giovanni Bellini. The texture there is notably thick; according to Julian Gascoigne, a specialist in British art at Sotheby’s, “a lot of that is knife work,” meaning that the paint was applied with a palette knife. It looks as fresh as cream. Gascoigne and I stood in front of the picture, the condition of which, barring a few cracks, is almost laughably untouched by time. No ill-advised Victorian restorations, no heavy varnishings, no smuts from candle smoke. Also, it’s unlined; that is to say, no extra backing was glued to the rear of the canvas to lend it support. (Such a process, as Gascoigne told me, “can seriously diminish the surface.”) The glow of many Turners has dwindled, thanks to unstable pigments, but here is an immaculate exception. Were its creator to see it now, he would presumably feel gratified. Indeed, as an inveterate meddler, he would probably pick up his brushes and carry on the good work.

The bidding for “Rome, from Mount Aventine,” in December, is unlikely to be as serene as the atmosphere that reigns within the frame. Having tempted prospective buyers during its global stops, the picture will have cranked up the force of their coveting. It is quite possible that, once sold, like “Salvator Mundi,” it will vanish from sight; I like to think that, in a nod to the family of its first owner, it might wind up on the walls of a Bond villain’s hideout, to complement his handsome gathering of tigers and sharks. (Keep in mind that a treasure that goes into a private collection can always come back out.) On the whole, though, it would be more fitting if, like a pilgrim, the painting found its way to Rome. “This is Turner’s love letter to the Rome that inspired the Grand Tour,” Gascoigne said to me. “More than just giving you a visual representation of the topography of the city, he’s trying to evoke the sensation of actually being there.”

As for the competition, it would be surprising if the Getty Museum, in Los Angeles, were not to enter the fray. “Rome, from Mount Aventine” would make a natural companion for “Modern Rome – Campo Vaccino,” another of Turner’s dreamlike cityscapes, from the same era, which the museum already owns. Reuniting the pair would be like getting Romulus back together with Remus. Both pictures were bought from Munro’s estate, in 1878, by Lord Rosebery, who could afford them, having recently taken the wise precaution of marrying a Rothschild; the couple went so far as to pause their honeymoon, in Scotland, to view the paintings. (As the new bride explained, in a letter, “Archie wanted to see the Turners.”) Rosebery was later to become the British Prime Minister, though for little more than a year. Painting being a more enduring art than politics, both “Modern Rome – Campo Vaccino” and “Rome, from Mount Aventine” stayed in his family for generations, until this century. The first went to the Getty, in 2010, and the second, in 2014, to buyers unnamed, for around forty million dollars.

But why fight for this Turner, the galleries and the billionaires will ask, rather than any other? Because, as Gascoigne said, “It is now one of the last great handful of masterpieces, particularly from the late period of his work, that remain in private hands.” Soon it will pass to other hands; for the moment, though not for long, it is out in the open. Go and see it on Madison Avenue, and, for good measure, observe how other people see it, too. In “Modern Painters,” Ruskin wrote, “I am fond of standing by a bright Turner in the Academy, to listen to the unintentional compliments of the crowd—‘What a glaring thing!’ ‘I declare I can’t look at it!’ ‘Don’t it hurt your eyes?’—expressed as if they were in the constant habit of looking the sun full in the face.” We all need dazzling these days. Catch the light while you can. ♦

title: Theresa Hak Kyung Cha’s Linguistic Art
author: @NewYorker
content:
Also: Bill Irwin and Rachel Bloom in Molière, a new movie from Kogonada, the torrid post-punk of Sweeping Promises, and more.

November 6, 2026

It’s taken me some days to write about Theresa Hak Kyung Cha’s show at Artists Space, because I didn’t want to face the fact that she’s no longer around to keep growing as an artist, a thinker, and a woman. Cha explored her deep interest in language among distinct cultures—including that of her native South Korea, where she grew up, and of the United States, where she moved, in 1962, when she was eleven—with video, performance, and multimedia installations. “Theresa Hak Kyung Cha: Multiple Offerings” (organized by the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive, and on through Nov. 21) is the first retrospective of Cha’s work in twenty-five years, and I can’t imagine a more beautiful curatorial vision. Everything about it—placement, context, sound, moving image—works to create a kind of holistic portrait of an artist who was as devoted to image as she was to language, and to show the ways in which each amplifies the other.

Indeed, her mysterious and uncategorizable book “Dictee,” from 1982, features a number of women talking, ranging from Joan of Arc to the artist’s mother, who lived through Japanese rule, when Korean could not be spoken in public. In “Dictee,” and in her performances, many of which are featured in “Multiple Offerings,” Cha’s and other women’s voices rise out of bodies that have lived through some form of oppression to come out on the other side as whole and true. One walks away from this historic show deeply moved by its singularity, and angry: in 1982, shortly before her first exhibition at Artists Space was scheduled to open, Cha, who was working on a series of photographs about her time employed at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, was murdered.—Hilton Als

Dance

The first part of “Adaku”—a dance-theatre trilogy by Okwui Okpokwasili and Peter Born that spools out a speculative vision rooted in a pre-colonial African village—ended with wailing, as a beloved daughter was caught up in the transatlantic slave trade. Part 2, “She Shivers with It,” which has its New York début at BAM, starts with that choral cry and fast-forwards into an alternate present, tapping into embodied memory to trace the lineage of the lost daughter. Amid two hundred feet of snaking red coil, the ritualistic performance lingers in pain but also mines the humor in a magical hairdresser.—Brian Seibert (BAM Fisher; Nov. 11-15.)

Dance

Paul Taylor Dance Company has lately diversified its repertory considerably. This season includes new and recent pieces by the resident artists Robert Battle and Lauren Lovette; an example of mid-century psychedelia by Alwin Nikolais; and “Messengers, Maidens and the End of Something Else,” by the jokey postmodernist Pam Tanowitz. A tongue-in-cheek exploration of the classical-music repertoire, the dance pairs the first and fourth movements of Schubert’s “Death and the Maiden” quartet with a bright palette of movement and color. Those who come for Taylor will be rewarded with rare revivals of “Arabesque,” from 1999, which is set to a Debussy composition that suggests prettiness but soon reveals something darker, and “Byzantium,” from 1984, which probes the degenerate sides of society.—Marina Harss (David H. Koch Theatre; through Nov. 22.)

Broadway

Molière collapsed onstage while performing the lead role of his last play, “The Imaginary Invalid,” and died hours later. That it’s a sendup of doctors and medicine is an irony worthy of its author. Brandon J. Dirden’s revival, for Roundabout, features Bill Irwin (who also adapted the text from Doug Skinner’s translation) as the lead: a perfectly healthy hypochondriac exploited by greedy, bullshitting physicians. Irwin’s performance is a marvel of physical and vocal comedy, complemented by Crystal A. Dickinson as his sweet-talking, gold-digging wife; Rachel Bloom as the sly servant who sees and fixes all; and a bloviating Brooks Ashmanskas, double-cast as two of the quacks. In its whirligig puncturing of pretense, this sumptuous production not only honors Molière’s spirit but makes it felt, offering us ninety minutes with him in comedy heaven.—Dan Stahl (Haimes; through Nov. 22.)

Off Broadway

In the new musical “Midnight,” Rail (Todrick Hall, who also wrote and directed), an enslaved Black man, falls in love with Richard (Jeremy Beloate), a white man he works for; in the second act, they swap social placements, so that Rail is the wealthy landowner and Richard the enslaved worker. (They remain in love.) Even if the songs go on twice as long as is necessary to the plot, the singing is a considerable pleasure, with Kennedy Caughell bringing a spirited assurance to her turn as Scarlet, an imperious Southern belle, while Charlotte Odusanya imbues Lily Rose—a young woman wooed by Rail’s “pretty eyes”—with a lambent sweetness. Hall’s ambitious show is concerned with racial legibility and manipulation, but he’s threading with a dull needle.—Rhoda Feng (Daryl Roth; through Jan. 3.)

Movies

Reappropriating the means of production after two elaborate movies, the director Kogonada filmed “Zi” in Hong Kong, shooting on the fly with a main cast of three and a scant crew to match. The results are as daring as the method; the title character, a Hong Kong-born violinist (Michelle Mao), is awaiting test results about a possible brain tumor. In a variation on Agnès Varda’s “Cléo from 5 to 7,” Zi has hallucinations—seeing flashes of her future self, as though mentally stuck in her own past—but a chance connection with an American wanderer (Haley Lu Richardson) and a Korean scientist (Jin Ha) offers hope: the trio’s lurching, passionate overnight ramble helps diagnose a metaphysical malady. The filmmaker’s ardently curious vision of the cityscape links inner lives to history, self-images to aesthetics.—Richard Brody (Metrograph through Nov. 15, and in limited release.)

Post-Punk

Since its inception, in 2019, the torrid band Sweeping Promises has been a project about the act of creating. Its partners, Lira Mondal and Caufield Schnug, started up on a whim when a jam sesh in an abandoned science lab conjured their first song, which became the title track for their 2020 début, “Hunger for a Way Out.” The band was imagined as a space beyond the duo’s other musical projects to “capture the exhilaration of writing songs in the moment,” as Mondal put it, and the music is governed primarily by impulses—it’s lo-fi and punk, possessing a free spirit and a resourceful nature. Their most recent album, “You Say I Romanticize,” reaffirms their core drive with songs more explicitly about committing to an artistic life.—Sheldon Pearce (Baby’s All Right; Nov. 11.)

Taran Dugal excavates cocktails in Bushwick.

Brooklyn night life is full of imposing figures: brutish bouncers, cool-kid carousers, the rare haughty bartender. But it wasn’t until this summer’s opening of the Museum, a low-lit cocktail lounge in Bushwick, that barflies had to contend with a T. rex—or, at least, a replica of one, whose skull is mounted on a table in the back room. On a recent weekend, three friends sat to the dino’s right, trying their best to ignore his unmistakable glower. They’d begun their evening in the Gift Shop, a cozy parlor up front serving drinks and finger foods, before making their way through the establishment’s Exhibition Hall, a narrow space lined with engraved skulls, Egyptian figurines, and a kaleidoscopic array of gemstones and crystals. In the back, the friends perused the menu, which consisted of cocktails inspired by different aspects of natural history. The most adventurous of the group ordered the Insectarium, an earthy honey-gin Negroni with a cricket-infused tincture, accompanied by a small piece of ant-ridden chocolate. The queasiest, looking away, opted for the Crystal Pass, a velvety Old-Fashioned incorporating oaky Scotch, bourbon, and mole sauce. The third friend, between sips of his Birds of the World (a tangy tequila-based concoction of elderflower, sunflower seeds, guava, and pineapple), began eavesdropping on a couple nearby, whose discussion had turned to mammalian politics. “Hyenas get a bad rep from ‘The Lion King,’ ” a man said to his date, “but they’re just kind of taking care of the leftovers, you know?” The eavesdropper, busy finishing a delectable pepper-chicken skewer, couldn’t agree more. Eventually, the place emptied out, and the trio took their leave to the hazy groove of a Khruangbin track. After all, the sun had set, the T. rex was still glowering, and one can never be too careful in a museum at night.

His writing appears in the New York Times and the New York Review of Books. A Guggenheim fellow, he teaches at Yale University.

title: Company of Heroes 3's Operation Torch DLC ships off to North Africa in November, for new missions based around the Allied landings
author: Mark Warren
content:
Patton of attack

Atten-shun! Company Of Heroes 3's got new single-player missions inbound via a DLC set during the Allies' 1942 invasion of North Africa. You'll take charge of American forces through a campaign steeped in second world war history that's designed to test your tactical nous and ability to upgrade fighting units to come out on top.It's out on November 25th.

As is made rather obvious by its name, the DLC depicts Operation Torch, which saw the Brits and yanks work together to invade Vichy France-controlled Algeria and Morocco. There's a "dramatic campaign arc that spans the opening invasion, the defeat at Kasserine, and the final assault on Hill 609", no doubt with copious mentions of names like Eisenhower and Patton across its 15 missions.

You'll don the boots of three American soldiers who're either in command or in the thick of the action on the battlefield, with devs Relic noting that their "perspectives reflect the hardships, losses, responsibilities, and lessons learned as they are forged into the fighting force that will liberate Europe".

In between the likes of urban tank battles and stealth ops, you'll pick upgrades earned through completing objectives, ensuring your troops fight in the manner that best suits your preferred tactical slant. For example, I assume you'll be able to go all-in on artillery if all you're after is some big booms that look impressive, but might prove useless if the enemy are safely tucked away in deep cover waving their middle fingers at your boys.

"Company Of Heroes 3 is a rip-roaring return to form and then some for Relic's much loved RTS, and its stirring orchestral score will have you beating your chest and yelling hoo-rah like only the best toy soldier fantasies can," former RPS commander-in-chief Katharine wrote of COH 3 on release in 2023. "If Relic can iron out some of those lingering campaign niggles, this could easily be an all-timer for WWII strategy buffs."

More recently, current boss Julian gave roguelite spin-off Company of Heroes 3: Final Stand a go, coming out with the impression that it's a shakeup which succeded in increasing his appreciation for the series.

title: Days Gone studio's next PlayStation exclusive to be revealed and released in 2027, and it's not a sequel to the 2019 zombie-based action game, according to new report
author: Sherif Saed
content:
Deacon of hope.

Sony's Bend Studio, perhaps one of its lesser discussed development houses, has apparently been deep in development on its next title. The game is reportedly set to be announced in 2027, and released in the same year.

That's according to MP1st, citing "people aware of what's happening at Bend". Like Days Gone, Bend's next game is in third-person. The title is said to include co-op support, but no live service elements.

The report doesn't say whether the game is based on a new IP or an existing one, but it does state that it's not a sequel to Days Gone. The game is apparently "much further along in development" than we realise, which isn't entirely surprising considering Bend has been quiet for years.

The seven years since the release of Days Gone in 2019 have been tumultuous for Bend Studio. The developer revealed in 2022 its next project is a new IP that "builds upon the open-world systems of Days Gone" and includes multiplayer elements.

Two years later, a job post described a game in development at Bend as a triple-A live service project. That unannounced game was then cancelled in 2025, triggering a wave of layoffs at the studio that took place a few months later. Bend hasn't said a word since then.

It's now clear the studio hopped on its next project following the cancellation of that live service game. Seeing as 2026 is nearly over, we're not likely to be waiting much longer to see that mysterious game unveiled.
